catalog_quote: 名詞の型の一覧を（7）に示す。アクセント単位が長くなっても 2 種類の対立しかない「二型アクセント」である。両系列を α／β と名付ける［…］ただし，1 拍語は α 系列の 1 種類のみである［…］α 系列は単語レベルでも文節レベルでも同じで，単語は裸の文節でもあるので，「文節がアクセント単位になり，その次末拍のみが低まる」と記述される。それに対して β 系列は単語レベルでの指定が必要で，（/[/）「単語の次末拍（−②）に昇り核がある」と解釈する。昇り核のある拍で高くなり，その後は，接続形ではそのまま「文節」の最後まで高く続くのに対して，言い切り形では文節末拍で下がる。［…］β 系列との対比上，α 系列は無核型と認められる［…］補足すると，β 系列の単語に固有なのは上昇（[）であり，下降（]）は単語に固有の属性ではない。 (pp. 51–53) — English abstract, p. 75: "the Wan dialect, which has a two-pattern accent system, one pattern with word-tone on the bunsetsu unit, and one pattern with an ascending kernel on the penultimate mora of the word. Here we see coexistence of word-tone and accent kernel. It also has the peculiarity that a moraic nasal can bear a final high pitch of the word-tone, but not an ascending kernel."

new_statements.translation: The list of noun patterns is given in (7). It is a 'two-pattern accent' with only two contrasting types no matter how long the accent unit becomes. I call the two series α/β [...] The α series is the same at word level and at bunsetsu (phrase) level, and since a word is also a bare bunsetsu, it is described as 'the bunsetsu is the accent unit and only its penultimate mora is lowered'. The β series, by contrast, needs a word-level specification, and is interpreted as 'having a rising kernel on the penultimate mora (−2) of the word'. The pitch rises at the kernel mora; after that, in the connective form it stays high to the end of the bunsetsu, whereas in the final (citation) form it falls on the last mora of the bunsetsu. [...] In contrast to the β series, the α series is recognised as the kernelless type. (English abstract, p. 75: 'the Wan dialect, which has a two-pattern accent system, one pattern with word-tone on the bunsetsu unit, and one pattern with an ascending kernel on the penultimate mora of the word.')

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kikai has an N-pattern (Ryukyuan-type) pitch accent, not stress. Each lexical item belongs to one of a small fixed number of accent series (two in Uwano 2012: α/β; Uwano 2016 and the NINJAL data papers add a third, γ). The pitch shape is fixed by the series and counted from the right edge: α = kernelless, the whole bunsetsu (noun + particles) is high except its penultimate mora, which is low; β = an obligatory pitch rise on the penultimate mora of the word (-2), high to the end of the phrase in connective form, with a fall on the phrase-final mora in citation form; γ = the rise on the antepenultimate mora (-3), 3+-mora words only. Mora (not syllable) is the counting unit. Nothing is said of stress/intensity; the description is entirely pitch/tonal.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not applicable; no secondary prominence is described. Uwano notes (pp. 52–53) that in the β series only the rise is lexical, the final fall being a phrase-final intonational feature.
new_statements.exceptions: One-mora (long-vowel) nouns are all α (p. 52); the moraic nasal can carry the α word-tone's final high but not a β rising kernel (abstract p. 75). Uwano 2016 p. 95 revises the 2012 two-pattern analysis of central/southern dialects to three-pattern after a γ pattern was found in loanwords and place names (mostly words with a moraic nasal/geminate in the penult); the northern Onotsu dialect is three-pattern and additionally sensitive to word length (≤3, 4, >4 morae) and special morae (Uwano 2016 pp. 97, 109). Shirata 2016 (abstract) analyses Kamikatetsu as a two-pattern system with accentedness lexically specified per morpheme and an HLH* melody.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the bunsetsu (word + following particles) for the α series and the word for the β/γ kernels; citation (言い切り) and connective (接続) forms differ for β/γ (final fall vs. sustained high). Data are elicited nouns in isolation and with particles; the Wan dialect (central Kikai, the most widespread type) is the reference variety, with Sakamine, Kamikatetsu, Araki, Nakasato and Isaneku compared.
new_statements.identity_note: Kikai (kika1239) is not a single accent system: the quoted statement describes the central/southern type, exemplified by the Wan dialect (the most widespread type on the island; Sakamine, Kamikatetsu, Araki, Nakasato, Isaneku described alongside), which Uwano 2012 analyses as two-pattern and Uwano 2016 revises to three-pattern (α/β/γ). The northern villages Onotsu, Shitooke and Sateku have a distinct three-pattern system with word-length and special-mora constraints (Uwano 2016; Uwano 2002b). Shirata 2016 (Kamikatetsu, southernmost village) analyses that variety as two-pattern with morpheme-level accentedness. No separate Glottolog codes exist for these dialect groups; all fall under kika1239.

sources.locator: §5.1 アクセント体系, pp. 51–53 (Wan dialect); English abstract p. 75
sources.note: Wan dialect (central Kikai) has a two-pattern (N-type) pitch accent: alpha series = phrase(bunsetsu)-level word-tone with only the penultimate mora low (kernelless); beta series = rising kernel on the penultimate mora of the word; five other central/southern dialects (Sakamine, Kamikatetsu, Araki, Nakasato, Isaneku) described relative to Wan (pp. 51–53, 75).

sources.citation: 上野善道 (Uwano, Zendo). 2016. 喜界島小野津方言のアクセント体系—外来語と地名語彙から見る—. 音声研究 (Journal of the Phonetic Society of Japan) 20(3): 95–111.
sources.note: p. 95: earlier view was central/south = two-pattern, north = three-pattern; a third (gamma) pattern has since been found in central/south too, so they are three-pattern; p. 97 (4) Nakasato: alpha = bunsetsu-domain, penultimate mora low (kernelless); beta = rising kernel on word penultimate mora (-2); gamma = rising kernel on antepenultimate mora (-3, 3+ mora words only); p. 109: Onotsu (north) confirmed three-pattern, sensitive to word length and special morae.

sources.citation: 上野善道 (Uwano, Zendo). 2013–2016. 喜界島方言のアクセント資料 (1)–(5). 国立国語研究所論集 (NINJAL Research Papers) 5: 121–154; 6: 183–216; 7: 289–310; 10: 265–295; 11: 181–213.
sources.note: Data volumes for central/southern dialects (Nakasato, Sakamine, Kamikatetsu): (4) abstract reports a third (gamma) pattern in nouns, so nouns as well as verbs are three-pattern (alpha/beta/gamma); (5) loanword accent, three patterns with heavy skew toward beta.
